title: India Votes Against UN Moratorium on Death Penalty, Citing Sovereign Right to Set Penalties
excerpt: The UNGA Third Committee adopted the Mexico-introduced draft 133-33, but India argued there is no international consensus against capital punishment and that Article 6 of the ICCPR permits it with restrictions.
body:
• India voted against a UN General Assembly draft resolution calling for a global moratorium on the death penalty, which the Third Committee adopted by 133 votes to 33, with 16 abstentions, on Friday, November 13, 2026.
  • India argued there is no international consensus against capital punishment, that Article 6 of the ICCPR permits it with restrictions, and that sovereign states decide their own penalties.
  • India supported a separate resolution on extrajudicial executions but disassociated itself from a paragraph it said equated lawful capital punishment with torture.
  • The vote continues India's position in 2016, 2018 and 2024; the draft now proceeds to the full General Assembly.

India has voted against a draft United Nations General Assembly resolution calling on nations to establish a moratorium on the death penalty, asserting that there is no international consensus against capital punishment and that every sovereign state has the right to determine its own legal system and penalties.

The 193-member General Assembly's Third Committee adopted the resolution, introduced by Mexico, by a recorded vote on Friday, November 13, 2026, with 133 countries voting in favour, 33 against and 16 abstaining, The Hindu reported. India voted against alongside Bahrain, China, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Japan, Kuwait, Maldives, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United States.

What the resolution asks

The resolution, titled "Moratorium on the use of the death penalty," expressed deep concern about the continued application of capital punishment and noted a significant surge in reported executions in 2025, while reaffirming the right of countries to develop their own legal systems in accordance with international law. It called on all states to establish a moratorium on executions with a view to abolishing the death penalty, to progressively restrict its use, and not to impose it for offences committed by persons below 18, on pregnant women, or on persons with mental or intellectual disabilities.

India's case

Speaking at the Third Committee's 43rd plenary meeting of the 81st General Assembly, Bhavika Mangalanandan, First Secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, said capital punishment in India is a statutory provision exercised only in the "rarest of rare" cases, with safeguards including mandatory confirmation of death sentences by a higher court.

"There is no international consensus against capital punishment, and article six of the ICCPR permits its use with restrictions. Capital punishment is meted out after rigorous and due legal process. It is therefore a travesty to term it state-inflicted death."

— Bhavika Mangalanandan, First Secretary, Permanent Mission of India to the UN

In the same session, India supported a separate draft resolution on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, but formally disassociated itself from its Operational Paragraph 6, which refers to a Special Rapporteur's report. Mangalanandan said India strongly disagreed with the assertion that the death penalty inherently constitutes torture or ill-treatment, and called it "disingenuous and mischievous" to discuss capital punishment under a resolution on extrajudicial executions. India stressed that extrajudicial executions are unlawful and a clear violation of human rights.

The other side

France welcomed the committee's adoption of the resolution by a large majority, describing it as an important step towards the universal abolition of the death penalty. The United States, which also voted against, supported Singapore's amendment on national sovereignty and said the decision on capital punishment must be addressed through the domestic democratic processes of individual states, consistent with international law.

India's vote against the biennial moratorium draft is consistent with its positions in 2016, 2018 and 2024, ANI reported. The committee's draft now goes forward for consideration by the full General Assembly.
nri_angle: The vote places India alongside the US, China and Japan in opposing a global executions pause, a position India has held at the UN since 2016.
